items.ja: 鶏白湯らーめん 塩「塩のキラメキ®」
items.romaji: tori-paitan raamen shio / Shio no Kirameki
items.note: Paitan (白湯) means the chicken bones were boiled hard enough to emulsify — thick, opaque, almost soup-like-gravy, not the clear broth most people expect. Kirameki mill their own noodles (自家製麺). Sizes on the board: 小 (ko, small) ¥800 / 並 (nami, regular) ¥850 / 大 (dai, large) ¥930 / 特大 (tokudai, extra large) ¥1,010 — point at the size word, they cost different amounts.

items.ja: 鶏白湯らーめん 醤油「醤油のキラメキ®」
items.romaji: tori-paitan raamen shouyu / Shouyu no Kirameki
items.note: Same thick chicken broth as the shio, but the seasoning base (タレ, tare) is soy sauce, so it is darker and rounder. Same size ladder: 小¥800 / 並¥850 / 大¥930 / 特大¥1,010.

items.ja: 極濃鶏白湯まぜそば GTM
items.en: Brothless noodles in ultra-thick chicken paitan sauce
items.note: GTM is the shop's own abbreviation. まぜそば (mazesoba) = 'mixed noodles': there is no soup, just a very reduced chicken sauce sitting at the bottom with the toppings. Stir it hard from the bottom before the first bite or the top half is dry. 小¥920 / 並¥970 / 大¥1,070 / 特¥1,170.

items.en: The GTM mazesoba loaded with everything
items.note: DX = デラックス, deluxe — the same bowl with extra chashu pork, a marinated egg, kimchi and sheets of nori piled on. 小¥1,220 / 並¥1,270 / 大¥1,370 / 特¥1,470.

items.ja: 麻辣シビカラ台湾まぜそば
items.note: 麻辣 (málà) is the Sichuan pairing of chilli heat (辣) with the tingling numbness of Sichuan pepper (麻); シビカラ is the Japanese slang for the same thing — shibireru (numb) + karai (hot). The flyer warns シビレル辛さがクセになる — 'the numbing heat is addictive'. Spicy by design; no mild version. 小/並¥950, 大/特¥1,050.

items.ja: 台湾まぜそば 直太朗
items.en: The plain Taiwan mazesoba — brothless noodles with spicy minced pork and raw egg yolk
items.note: Despite the name, 台湾まぜそば is a Nagoya invention. No soup: chilli-hot minced pork (台湾ミンチ), chives, garlic, nori and a raw yolk sit on thick noodles over a pool of tare. Break the yolk, stir everything hard, then eat. When about a third is left, ask for 追い飯 (oimeshi) — a scoop of rice tipped into the leftover sauce — if the shop offers it that day. 小/並/大¥900, 特¥1,000, メガ (mega) ¥1,000.

items.en: Taiwan mazesoba with the full topping load
items.note: Same bowl as the 直太朗 plus chashu, two egg halves, kimchi and extra nori. 小/並¥1,160, 大/特¥1,260.

items.ja: 台湾まぜそば 豚キムチーズ
items.en: Taiwan mazesoba with pork, kimchi and melting cheese
items.note: 豚 (buta, pork) + キムチ (kimchi) + チーズ (cheese), squashed into one word. Shredded cheese melts into the hot noodles and takes the edge off the chilli. 小/並¥1,060, 大/特¥1,160.

items.en: House topping set: +2 slices pork, +1 marinated egg, +3 sheets of nori
items.note: The flyer spells out exactly what you get: 肉+2枚・煮玉子+1個・海苔+3枚. Comes in a 塩 version and a まぜそば version — say which bowl you ordered. Note that on the Kirameki Special the chashu already in the bowl is increased rather than added on top.
増量 (zouryou) is the word to look for on any Japanese menu — it means 'increased quantity' of whatever precedes it.
Shredded cheese for melting into a mazesoba. Only served on the wheat noodles, so it is not a gluten-free option in practice.
Also written 味玉 (ajitama) elsewhere — the same thing: a jammy-yolked egg steeped in a soy-and-mirin marinade. The marinade is soy sauce, which in Japan is wheat-brewed by default.
The chilli-and-garlic minced pork that defines a Taiwan mazesoba — order more of it if you want the bowl hotter.
ネギ (negi) is the green onion piled on almost every bowl. Cheap way to cut the richness of a paitan broth.
枚 (mai) is the counter for flat things — 3枚 is three sheets. Nori itself is just seaweed, but it goes into a wheat-noodle bowl here.

items.en: Japanese fried chicken + rice, added to any noodle order
items.note: The big red flash on the flyer reads お好きな麺類＋270円 — 'any noodle dish you like, plus ¥270' — and 終日お得 means the deal runs all day, not just at lunch. Kara-age is marinated in soy and dusted in wheat/potato starch before frying.

items.en: Rice bowl topped with the shop's pork and spring onion
items.note: 丼 (don/donburi) = a bowl of rice with something on top. Add-on price when ordered with any noodle dish.
Add-on price with any noodle dish. Kimchi in Japan is usually seasoned with fish sauce or dried shrimp as well as soy.

items.en: Plain white rice, regular or large
items.note: Plain unseasoned steamed rice — genuinely safe on both counts as long as nothing is poured over it. 並 = regular, 大 = large; the flyer prices both at ¥170.

items.en: Fried chicken, sold by the piece
items.note: 個 (ko) is the counter for small round things — 1個 is one piece, so you can order exactly as many as you want. Soy marinade plus a flour/starch coating.

kyr_men_to_sake_no_tora.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Core menu prices read from photographs of the shop's own printed menu card and paper order sheet dated July 2026; the 酒と寅のアテ side-dish list is from an October 2025 photograph of the same menu folder.

items.note: 汁あり literally means 'with liquid'. Supervised by Kyoto tantanmen house 金鶏楼 and marked 人気NO.1！まずはこれ！ — 'most popular, start here'. You do not order verbally: staff hand you an オーダーシート (order sheet) and you circle your choices. On it you set 麺のかたさ (noodle firmness: かため firm / 基本 standard / やわめ soft), ねぎ (spring onion: なし none / あり yes), 肉味噌 (minced-pork miso: なし / あり), then two 0–5 dials — 辣油 (rāyu, chilli oil; 2 is 基本, the default) and 花椒 (huājiāo, Sichuan pepper, the numbing one; 1 is default). Circle 基本 everywhere if you are unsure — the sheet itself says the standard settings are recommended for first-timers. A half portion, 汁ありハーフサイズ, is ¥800.

汁なし = 'no liquid'. Sesame paste, chilli oil and minced pork sit in the bottom of the bowl with no broth at all — stir hard from the bottom before the first bite or you eat plain noodles then a puddle of sauce. Two extra options unlock on the order sheet for this version only: 葱油 (negi-abura, spring-onion oil) and フライドオニオン (crisp fried onion), each なし/あり. The menu note お酒にもごはんにも合います means it goes with both the sake and a bowl of rice — ordering a 白ごはん to mop the bowl out is the intended finish.
夏季限定 = summer only (in 2026 from 14 May), 一日限定10食 = ten bowls a day, then it is gone. Served with a mortar so you grind the sesame yourself and a citrus wedge to squeeze over — 胡麻をお好みにすり、柑橘をギュッと絞って.

The menu states 動物由来原料不使用 — 'no animal-derived ingredients' — and describes the base as お昆布とお豆さんのチカラ, 'the power of kombu and beans', i.e. kelp stock and soy instead of the usual pork-and-chicken. That is the shop's own written claim and it is unusually explicit for Japan, where hidden bonito dashi is the norm; still worth confirming the chilli oil is the plain one. Wheat noodles, so not gluten-free. Spice level adjustable like the others.

items.en: Kids' dan dan noodles (not spicy) with a toy
items.note: からくない汁あり担担麺＋おもちゃ — the soup version with the heat taken out, plus a toy. Also the fallback if you cannot handle chilli at all.

items.en: Slow-cooked soft egg, added on top
items.note: 温泉玉子 (onsen tamago), short form 温玉 — cooked slowly at low temperature so the white is barely set and the yolk is custardy. Break it into a soupless bowl and it turns the sauce creamy.
追い (oi-) as a prefix means 'chase it with more' — you will meet it again as 追い飯 (extra rice) and 追いしば漬け below. Written ねぎ増し on the wall menu.
大盛 (oomori) is the standard Japanese word for an upsized portion — you will see it on every noodle menu in the country. Here it is spelled out as 1.5倍, one and a half times.
しば漬け is one of Kyoto's three classic pickles: aubergine and cucumber salted with red shiso leaf, magenta and sharply sour. A local touch on a Sichuan dish — the acidity cuts the sesame fat.
肉味噌 is pork mince fried down with miso and aromatics — the savoury heart of a tantanmen. The order sheet notes it is made with 花椒 (Sichuan pepper).

items.en: The gritty sediment from the chilli oil, for extra heat
items.note: 滓 (kasu) is the solid dregs left at the bottom of the chilli-oil jar — chilli flakes and aromatics, far hotter than the oil itself. 辛増 = more heat. Fifty yen, and the cheapest way to make the bowl serious.

items.en: Add 2 pieces of fried chicken + a small rice to any tantanmen
items.note: The set price is the ADD-ON, not the total: お好きな担担麺＋鶏の唐揚げ2個＋ごはん小 — 'the tantanmen of your choice, plus two pieces of kara-age, plus a small rice'.

items.en: Add 2 fried chicken wings + a small rice
items.note: 手羽 (teba) is the chicken wing; 手羽から is the shop's contraction of 手羽唐揚げ, fried wings. 寅 (Tora, 'tiger') is the shop's own name attached to its signature version.

items.en: Add 2 boiled dumplings + a small rice
items.note: 水餃子 = boiled (not pan-fried) dumplings, thicker and slippery-skinned. Wheat wrappers, soy in the filling.

items.en: Rice topped with minced-pork miso and a soft egg
items.note: The house rice bowl. Three sizes: 小 (small) ¥500 / 中 (chū, medium) ¥550 / 大 (large) ¥600 — 小・中・大 is the size ladder you will see everywhere in Japan.

items.ja: 白ごはん（八代目儀兵衛）
items.en: Plain white rice, from Kyoto rice merchant Hachidaime Gihei
items.note: 白ごはん = plain steamed white rice, nothing added — genuinely gluten-free and vegan. 八代目儀兵衛 is a well-known Kyoto rice shop, so this is better rice than the usual side. 小¥200 / 中¥250 / 大¥300. Order one to finish a 汁なし bowl with.

たたき (tataki) means the outside is flashed over high heat and the inside left raw, then sliced and served cold with a ponzu-type sauce. アテ (ate) is Kansai slang for a small dish eaten with drink — the Tokyo word is おつまみ. Ponzu contains soy sauce.
Chicken marinated in soy, sake and ginger, dusted in starch and flour, fried twice. 個 (ko) counts the pieces.

items.en: The house fried chicken wings, 3 pieces
items.note: Wings rather than thigh meat — more skin, more to gnaw, better with beer.
Same starch-and-flour treatment as fried chicken, applied to octopus — chewy inside, crisp outside.

items.en: Spring rolls with whatever is in season
items.note: 季節の (kisetsu no) = 'of the season' — the filling changes through the year, so ask what is in them today. Wheat wrapper.
水 (mizu/sui) = water — boiled, not fried. Slippery thick skins, eaten with a vinegar-and-soy dip.
焼き (yaki) = grilled/fried — the familiar crisp-bottomed gyoza. Wheat wrapper, soy in the filling and the dip.

items.en: Cold tofu, the shop's 'most fearsome' version
items.note: 冷奴 (hiyayakko) is chilled block tofu, normally a mild dish with ginger and soy. 最恐 is a pun — 最強 means 'strongest', but written with 恐 (fear) it means 'scariest', i.e. this one is loaded with chilli. Toppings usually include soy sauce and often bonito flakes, so confirm before treating it as vegan.
杏仁豆腐 is not tofu at all — it is a set milk pudding flavoured with apricot kernel, the standard Chinese-restaurant dessert. やわらか = soft-set. Usually made with dairy and sometimes gelatine.

kyr_aji_no_tentoku_kyoto_shi.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read from a January 2026 photograph of this branch's own ticket machine; the operator's corporate site publishes no prices for any branch, so nothing here is imported from another shop.

items.note: The whole reason the shop exists. 油そば = 'oil noodles': NO SOUP. A secret soy tare and blended vegetable oils sit hidden under the noodles; chashu, menma, spring onion, nori and half an egg go on top. THE RITUAL: stir hard from the bottom first, then reach for the two big bottles on the counter — お酢 (osu, vinegar) and ラー油 (rāyu, chilli oil) — and add a circuit of each, then stir again. The shop's own instruction card says the vinegar is the key (ポイントはお酢). There is grated garlic (おろしにんにく) in a pot on the counter too. Buy a ticket at the 券売機 (ticket machine) BEFORE sitting; the machine takes only OLD-style banknotes and will not accept the new ¥500 coin — hand new notes to the owner to swap. Machine price ¥850 = ¥773 + ¥77 tax.
Same bowl, salt-based tare instead of soy — lighter and cleaner, and reviewers describe it as the richer-tasting of the two despite that. Same vinegar-and-chilli-oil ritual.

items.ja: 油そば　醤油味　大盛
items.note: 大盛 (oomori) = large. The shop has historically sold this as ダブル/320g — double noodles for the same amount of tare, so it eats drier; add a little more vinegar. Its size names are worth knowing if you see them written out: ひかえめ/ハーフ 80g, ていばん/シングル 160g, まんぷく/ダブル 320g, はらきれ/トリプル 480g — literally 'modest', 'standard', 'full belly', 'burst stomach'.

items.ja: 油そば　塩味　大盛
items.note: Double noodles, salt tare. Machine price ¥1,100 = ¥1,000 + ¥100 tax.

items.ja: 油そば　シンプル　塩味
items.en: Stripped-back abura-soba — noodles and tare, minimal toppings
items.note: シンプル (simple) is the bare version without the full topping load. Regulars order it as a 〆 (shime) — the noodle dish that closes a night of drinking, which is exactly what this shop is for: it opens at 18:00 and runs to 23:00.

items.ja: ライスセット　醤油
items.en: Soy abura-soba with a bowl of rice
items.note: The English on the button reads 'Original sauce noodles, soy sauce taste, with rice'. The rice is there to be tipped into the bowl at the end to mop up the leftover tare — the same idea as 追い飯 (oimeshi) at a mazesoba shop.

items.en: Salt abura-soba with a bowl of rice
items.note: Same set, salt tare.

Machine price ¥380 = ¥345 + ¥35 tax. The counter has a 餃子たれ (gyoza dip) bottle alongside the vinegar and chilli oil. Wheat wrappers and soy in both filling and dip. The top row of the machine also carries two ¥1,200 buttons whose pictures pair a plate of these gyoza with a bowl of abura-soba — that is the noodles-plus-gyoza set, if you want both. Their kanji labels were too blurred in the photograph to transcribe, so they are not listed here as separate items.

玉 (tama) is the counter for a portion-ball of noodles — 1玉 is one serving's worth. The button's English reads 'One noodles addition'. Different from 替玉 (kaedama, a refill served later at a tonkotsu shop): here you buy it up front and it comes in the same bowl.
Labelled in English on the machine as 'Boiled egg, soy sauce taste' — which tells you plainly that it has been steeped in wheat-brewed soy.

items.ja: トッピング　キムチ
items.note: Its acidity works like the vinegar, cutting the oil. Japanese kimchi usually contains fish sauce or dried shrimp as well as soy.

items.en: The whole surface covered in shredded nori
items.note: きざみ (kizami) = shredded; 一面 (ichimen) = the entire surface; まし (mashi) = extra. Plain seaweed, but it goes into a wheat-noodle bowl.

items.ja: クリスピーフライドオニオン
items.note: Fifty yen for a handful of crunch — the cheapest button on the machine and worth pressing. Fried onion is normally dusted in wheat flour.
チャーシュー (chāshū) is the braised/roasted pork loin that tops ramen; chopped small and heaped on rice with its own sauce. The machine's English reads 'Roasted pork rice bowl'.

A plain rice button sits in the small-button block; the price was not legible in the photograph of the machine, so check it on the day. Unseasoned steamed rice is safe on both counts — just don't let anyone ladle tare over it.
生 (nama) = 'raw', i.e. draught rather than bottled. Note the sign taped above the machine: the shop asks each customer to order one noodle dish and will not seat you for drinks alone.
There are also oolong tea (ウーロン茶) and Calpis (カルピス, a sweet milky soft drink) buttons on the same block.

kyr_ryouriya_terado.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Sushi and grill prices from the shop's own October 2025 menu posting; curry tsukemen prices from its own May 2025 posting. The shop now serves dinner only (17:00–22:00, closed Mondays), so the curry tsukemen that used to be a lunch dish is an evening order.

items.ja: ９貫握り寿司　味噌汁付き
items.en: Nine pieces of hand-pressed sushi, with miso soup
items.note: 貫 (kan) is the counter for a piece of nigiri — 九貫 is nine pieces, chef's selection. 味噌汁付き means miso soup is included (付き = 'comes with'). The shop prints its menu in Japanese, English, Chinese and Korean, so you can point. The sushi rice is fine; the soy sauce you dip in is wheat-brewed, and miso is often barley — bring your own tamari if that matters.

items.ja: ８貫握り寿司　味噌汁付き
items.en: Eight pieces of hand-pressed sushi, with miso soup
items.note: The same set one piece smaller — the standard order here.

雲丹 (uni) is sea urchin roe — creamy, briny, faintly sweet, and the single most expensive thing per bite in most sushi bars. Wrapped in a band of nori (軍艦, gunkan style) so it doesn't slide off. One piece, so you can try it without committing.
盛り合わせ (moriawase) = an assortment on one plate, chosen by the chef from what came in that day. Raw fish only, no rice. Soy sauce for dipping = wheat.

items.ja: 雲丹海鮮ちらし丼　味噌汁付き
items.en: Rice bowl scattered with sea urchin and mixed seafood, with miso soup
items.note: ちらし (chirashi) means 'scattered' — instead of individual nigiri, the fish is strewn over a bowl of seasoned sushi rice. 海鮮 (kaisen) = seafood generally. Easier to eat than nigiri if you are tired of chopstick precision.

items.ja: まぐろ５貫握りウニ乗せ
items.en: Five pieces of tuna nigiri, each crowned with sea urchin
items.note: 乗せ (nose) = 'placed on top'. The showpiece of the counter — lean red tuna with a spoonful of uni on each piece.
マグロ (maguro) is tuna — the default red-fleshed sushi fish. Five of the same, if you know what you like.
The safest order for a nervous first-timer, and the cheapest of the five-piece sets.

items.en: Half a wooden tray of Hokkaido sea urchin
items.note: Sold as 半箱, half of the flat wooden box (折 ori) that uni is graded and shipped in from Hokkaido — the tongues laid out in rows, eaten as they are. A splurge item, priced accordingly.

items.en: Salmon grilled in sweet Kyoto white miso
items.note: 西京 is an old name for Kyoto ('the western capital') and 西京味噌 is its pale, low-salt, very sweet rice-koji miso. The fish is buried in it for a day or two, then grilled — the miso caramelises and the flesh turns dense and sweet. One of the genuinely Kyoto things on this menu. Saikyo miso is normally rice-based rather than barley, but confirm, and the marinade usually contains mirin and sake.
Raw fish and prawn over leaves with a Japanese dressing — those are almost always soy- or dashi-based.
Prawn and vegetables in a light wheat-flour batter, with a lemon wedge. The dipping sauce, 天つゆ (tentsuyu), is dashi plus soy — so bonito and wheat both.

items.en: Noodles served dry, dipped into a curry broth
items.section: カレーつけ麺のメニュー
items.note: The dish that makes a Japanese restaurant show up under 'ramen' searches. つけ麺 (tsukemen) means the noodles arrive cold and naked on one plate and a small bowl of hot concentrated soup arrives beside them — you dip a few strands at a time rather than pouring it over. What makes this one Kyoto and not a ramen shop is the broth: the menu says お出汁の効いたカレースープ, a curry built on 出汁 (dashi, the kelp-and-bonito stock that underlies all Japanese cooking) rather than on stock cubes. Comes with chicken, half an egg, pickled radish and grilled vegetables. The shop also sells the soup frozen.

items.ja: 豚しゃぶカレーつけ麺
items.en: Curry tsukemen with cold poached pork
items.section: カレーつけ麺のメニュー
items.note: Marked 店主おすすめ — the owner's recommendation. しゃぶ from しゃぶしゃぶ: paper-thin pork swished through hot water for a few seconds and then chilled, so it stays soft. The menu calls the pork カレーと相性抜群, 'a superb match for the curry'.

items.ja: 魚の天ぷら付　カレーつけ麺
items.en: Curry tsukemen with a side of fish tempura
items.section: カレーつけ麺のメニュー
items.note: 付 (tsuki) = 'comes with'. The fish changes with the season — in summer it is often 鱧 (hamo, pike conger), the Kyoto summer fish whose fine bones have to be scored by hand before cooking. Described as サクッと軽い食感, light and crisp.

items.en: Curry tsukemen with beef and raw spring onion
items.section: カレーつけ麺のメニュー
items.note: 牛 (gyuu) beef with シャキシャキねぎ — shaki-shaki is the onomatopoeia for a crisp, squeaky-fresh crunch, so the onion is raw and heaped, not wilted. The most expensive of the four.

items.section: カレーつけ麺 トッピング
items.note: Order this with a curry tsukemen and tip it into the leftover dipping broth at the end — the standard tsukemen finish. Plain steamed rice with nothing on it is genuinely gluten-free and vegan.

items.section: カレーつけ麺 トッピング
items.note: 小 = small, 中 = medium. Same rice, bigger bowl.

items.section: カレーつけ麺 トッピング
items.note: 大盛 (oomori) = large; 玉 (tama) is the counter for a ball of noodles, so 1.5玉 is one and a half servings. Only ¥110 more.
